# One convolution, split in two

A 3×3 convolution from 32 channels to 64 does two jobs at once: it looks at a
**neighbourhood**, and it **mixes channels**. Every output channel gets its own 3×3 window
into every input channel, which is 32 × 64 × 9 = **18,432 weights**.

Split it up. First a 3×3 that looks at neighbourhoods but never mixes — `groups` set equal
to the channel count, so each channel gets exactly one filter of its own: 32 × 9 = **288
weights**. Then a 1×1 that mixes channels but sees no neighbourhood at all: 32 × 64 =
**2,048 weights**.

**2,336 against 18,432, for the same input and the same output shape.** That is `groups`,
one widget, doing the whole of MobileNet.

## What it costs, across a whole network

| network | parameters | validation |
|---|---|---|
| ordinary convolutions | **539,178** | 0.6095 ± 0.014 |
| depthwise separable | **67,914** | 0.5925 ± 0.004 |

**7.9× fewer weights.** That number is arithmetic, not measurement — it comes out of the
shapes and cannot vary.

The accuracy line is measurement, and it deserves a weaker verb. 0.5925 against 0.6095 is a
gap of 0.017, which is about one spread of the larger model across two seeds. The honest
claim is **"it did not collapse"**, not "it cost nothing" — two seeds is not enough to put a
number that small beyond doubt, and elsewhere in this pack a 3-seed result has already been
overturned by an 8-seed one.

What is beyond doubt is the trade being offered: an eighth of the memory, for a difference
you have to squint at.

## Why this is everywhere and you have never noticed

Every phone that runs a camera model in real time runs something shaped like the bottom row.
The saving is not really the parameter count — it is the **memory traffic**. A depthwise
convolution touches each channel once, and on hardware where moving numbers costs more than
multiplying them, that is the whole game.

The catch is that the two halves are individually weak. A depthwise layer cannot combine
what it sees across channels, and a 1×1 cannot see sideways. They only work **in the pairs
you see here**, and the pairing has to be repeated to reach the same expressiveness — which
is why the separable row has twice as many nodes for a fifth of the weights.
